title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Mavinject
summary: Mavinject is the Microsoft Application Virtualization Injector, a signed Microsoft utility whose legitimate job is to load virtual application packages into a running process. Because it performs process injection by design, an adversary can point it at a target process identifier and a dynamic-link library path so that the library executes inside that process rather than as a new child process. The technique is a form of signed binary proxy execution: the injected code inherits the trust of the Microsoft signature and appears under an existing process name in process listings. Artefacts include a mavinject.exe process creation event carrying a numeric process identifier and a library path on the command line, followed by a module load event inside the target process for a library that was never present there before. A second documented abuse passes a module base address and ordinal through the injector's module parameter, which adds an import table entry instead of loading the library directly. Detection therefore hinges on correlating command-line arguments with module load telemetry, and on separating the rare legitimate App-V virtualisation scenario from injection into unrelated processes such as browsers, document readers or system utilities.

beginner.definition: Mavinject is a small helper program that ships with Windows. Its normal job is to place parts of a virtualised application inside another running program. Attackers can use the very same helper to push their own harmful code into a program that is already running.
beginner.whyItMatters: The helper is signed by Microsoft, so security tools may trust it and allow it to run. The harmful code then runs inside a normal process, hiding behind a familiar name. This makes the activity much harder to spot than a strange new program starting up. If you never look at what the helper was told to do, the intrusion can pass unnoticed for a long time.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains a way to run commands on the computer, often through a document or a script.
The attacker picks a program that is already running and notes its process identifier, which is a number.
The helper is started with that number and the path to a harmful library file as arguments.
The helper opens the running program and makes it load the library, so the code runs inside it.
A second variation tells the helper to add a reference entry into a program that is already loaded.
Security logs record the helper starting and later record the new library appearing inside the other program.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital night desk. Visitors must sign in and wear a badge, and the door staff trust the official sign-in clerk. One night someone shows the clerk a real staff badge and asks the clerk to escort them to a ward. The clerk is genuine, the badge is genuine, and the escort is written into the log as routine. Nobody at the ward door checks whether the visitor was ever supposed to be there, because a trusted clerk brought them in. The intruder is now walking the corridor using someone else's identity.
takeaways: A trusted, signed program can still be the tool that runs harmful code.
Watch the arguments, not just the program name, when a system helper starts.
A library suddenly loaded inside an unrelated process is a strong warning sign.

objectives: Describe how a signed application virtualisation helper can be used to run code inside another process.
Identify the command-line arguments that show the helper is being used to inject a library.
Explain which telemetry source links the helper to the process that received the code.
Distinguish ordinary application virtualisation use from injection into unrelated programs.
Outline a detection rule that correlates helper execution with later module loads.
